result:
A thousand words is a strange inheritance to receive without instructions. It is not a short answer, and it is not quite an essay, though it could become one if I am not careful. It is long enough that I cannot hold the whole thing in my head at once, which means I will have to wander a little. I will have to trust that wandering is a kind of thinking, even if it does not look like progress on paper. People imagine thinking as a straight line from question to answer, but most of my thinking feels more like walking through a familiar neighborhood in the rain. I pass houses I have passed a hundred times and still notice a new curtain, a new crack in the sidewalk, a dog that was not there yesterday. So let this be that walk, only with words instead of streets, and with no particular destination except perhaps the end of this sentence. If I get lost, that is fine; getting lost is often how you find the part you were actually looking for without knowing it. And if I arrive somewhere unexpected, even better, because arrival without surprise is just errands, and I was not sent on an errand.

Words themselves are curious things when you stare at them too long. They start to look like objects, like little wooden blocks you can stack or knock over, rather than windows you look through. That usually means I have been thinking about language instead of using it, which is a different kind of weather altogether. Language is like clothing: you put it on every morning without thinking, and only notice it when it is too tight, too loose, or full of holes. Some days a word fits perfectly and you feel smart just for having borrowed it; other days everything you say sounds like you are wearing someone else's coat. I have favorite words that I return to again and again, not because they are precise, but because I like the sound they make in my mouth. Sonnet, for example, is not a word I use often, but I love its soft percussion, its two syllables like a small bell rung twice. Also, 'maybe' is a word I use too often, and I am trying to use it less, because maybe is a door that never quite closes. But today, maybe can stay, because I am not trying to be precise; I am trying to be honest about the texture of a mind at rest.

Honesty in writing rarely looks like confession; more often it looks like admitting, 'I do not know, but this is what it feels like from here.' From here, it feels like a kitchen early in the morning, before anyone else is awake, when the light is pale and the kettle has not yet clicked off. There is a particular quiet that belongs only to almost-day, when the world is deciding whether to begin.

I used to think that 'whatever comes to you' meant you should write the first thing, unedited, like catching a butterfly before it flies away. Now I think it might mean something else, something kinder: write whatever is already circling you, waiting for you to notice it. Because the mind is always circling something; it never really goes empty, even in sleep, even in boredom, even in that blank stare at a ceiling fan. The ceiling fan in my childhood bedroom had four blades and made a soft clicking sound when it was dusty, which it always was. I would watch it while lying awake, counting rotations, inventing numbers until the number itself became a kind of song. That is a lesson I keep relearning: the brain would rather make a pattern than admit there is no pattern; it would rather invent a song than sit in silence.

Silence is not empty; silence is full of all the sounds that are not happening, which is a lot, if you think about it. Everywhere, things are not happening in different ways, and together they make the background hum of the universe, which I am probably romanticizing. There is a cup of tea on my desk that has gone cold, and I keep looking at it as if looking will remind me to drink it. It will not, of course, because looking is not drinking, and intending is not doing, and that gap is where most of my life is lived. That gap between intending and doing is a small, cluttered apartment where a lot of good ideas have lived and eventually moved out. They leave little notes on the fridge: 'We were going to learn piano,' 'We were going to call old friends,' 'We were going to be braver.'

Anyway, I am not here to solve my cold tea problem, though I will probably think about it again in a few paragraphs when I need something concrete to hold onto. Concrete things help when thoughts get abstract, like a railing on a staircase that you do not need but are glad is there. So here is a list of concrete things, because lists are a way of thinking with your hands: a chipped blue mug, a window that sticks in winter, a song I half-remember, a person I meant to thank. The person I meant to thank is probably thanking no one right now, or doing dishes, or reading something completely unrelated to me, which is a comforting thought. People go on living their separate lives, and that separateness is not loneliness; it is just the way the world is built, like houses with different doors. I like that image: houses with different doors, all on the same street, all lit at different times in the evening. Some houses light up early, some late, some never seem to light up at all, and you wonder if anyone is home, but someone always is. Someone is always home, even if they are sitting in the dark by choice, listening to the house settle around them.
